epilogue.title: Epilogue
epilogue.one:
After our recent conversation, I have taken the liberty of cross-referencing certain texts within Miskatonic's restricted collections. It may interest you to know that your account is not without precedent—though I doubt it will bring you much comfort. Firstly, on the matter of “Maddalena Talenti.” The name appears frequently in Charles Godfrey Leland’s Aradia, which claims Maddalena was a mortal woman who served as a disciple of Aradia, the “daughter of Diana,” a figure often associated with witchcraft in southern Europe. If such a woman did exist, she would be very old. The notion that she was the brazen young woman you traveled with is, to put it diplomatically, somewhat complex. Which brings me to the Three Mothers. Your descriptions align disturbingly well with fragmented accounts found in older enochian texts. If they have been defeated, know that you are not the first to do so. Accounts suggest they have been “unmade” more than once across the centuries, only to reappear once more.

On that subject, there is a particular theory I am compelled to share. There exists a school of thought-mostly among religious scholars-that the Three Mothers are not agents of cruelty. Instead, they are viewed as “custodians” appointed by a higher force, perhaps as instruments of providence. In this view, the sorrows they sow are not acts of malice but trials, meant to test those in whom they see worth. Consider, then, the nature of your struggle. Did they truly seek to destroy you, or did they seek to forge you? I make no claim to know the answer, but ask that you reflect on it yourself.

I wish I could offer more certainty. Take solace, perhaps, in this: whatever the Three Mothers’ motives may be, you stood before them and endured. In a tale as old as theirs, that alone is something worthy of record.

With admiration, Dr. Henry Armitage
epilogue.two:
I write to you with a heart full of concern, having pondered the account you were kind enough to share with me. As for these “Three Mothers” you mention, I must confess my ignorance—but the name of Herodias is infamous in the Holy Word. She was the wife of Herod Antipas and mother to Salome, remembered most vividly for her role in the death of John the Baptist. To most, she is a symbol of pride, cunning, and the peril of unchecked desire. Yet, there is another tale that Herodias was a priestess of Trivia, the Grecian goddess Hekate in her Roman aspect. If this is true, then perhaps Herodias’s ambitions extended beyond mortal politics.

I am troubled, too, by the role you say you have played in this story. If this Maddalena was indeed Herodias, she required you to enact her vengeance on her enemies. Why? If she possessed the means to harness or usurp these forces, why turn to you for aid? Doctrine does not paint her as one to seek out companions or followers lightly—instead, she likely sought instruments to carry out her will where she could not. That the majority of your correspondence took place within this ‘astral’ realm you describe should not be discounted. I say this not to accuse you, but to ready you for what challenges may yet come.

I have no simple answers to offer. But I will offer this counsel: Pray. Not necessarily to God (though you know I’d welcome that) but to whichever power brings you peace and clarity. Sometimes, in silence, we hear the loudest answers. Remember—my door is open, and my lantern is lit. Come by South Church if you need a place to rest your head, or simply to enjoy one of Viola’s meals.

Yours in faith and vigilance, Father Michael Gascoigne Presiding Minister of South Church, Arkham, MA
epilogue.three:
I hope this letter finds you well. I know it’s been some time since we last spoke, I've seen it in the shift of the world’s breath. Magic has returned. Real, living magic—the kind that flows from the ground like a wellspring, not from chanted words from a book or from rattled bones. And I know you had a hand in it. The Three Mothers endure, but they're not what they were. Hekate walks again, unbound and whole. The weight of that truth is too vast for me to see clearly, but I know what it means in the now: she’s no longer some distant, unknowable figure, torn into parts by an ungrateful disciple. She's free, here with us, and it’s all thanks to you.

I'd be lying if I said I knew exactly what's to come. Hekate’s mercy is a fleeting, fickle thing—but she’s already shown you one kindness, hasn’t she? She’s let you go home to a world that's still turning. I hope you understand the meaning of that gesture. Very few walk away from the crossroads intact.

Rest easy, if you're able, In this world, change takes time. That means that no one will whisper your names in reverence or place laurels on your brow while you live for what you've done. But I will remember.

'll keep the candle burning for you as long as it takes for the world to catch up. With gratitude and all the knowing in my heart, Anna Kaslow
epilogue.finlay: Finlay’s Model T putters to a halt at the curb, its engine's soft rattle cutting through the evening quiet. Finlay steps out, hat in hand, his face lit by the glow of a nearby streetlamp. There's a weight to his gaze—gratitude buried under exhaustion. He still looks better than the last time you saw him. “Thought I'd try to find you for a drink before you got into any more trouble,” he says, offering a crooked smile. “Don't think anyone else’ll ever know what we pulled off.” He glances away for a moment, tapping the brim of his hat against his leg. “But at least we'll always remember what happened, right? I don’t want to forget what we did. What you did.” For a man of few words, it's practically a sermon.
epilogue.naomi: Before you can respond, Naomi leans halfway out of the car’s window. 7 “You lovebirds gonna start necking, or can we get going?” she says, eyes flashing with mischief. “Peter's gonna throw a fit if we're late.” Finlay’s cheeks go redder than you've ever seen them, and he pulls his cap down low, muttering something sharp under his breath. Without another word, he climbs back into the driver's seat. The Model T rumbles back to life, and with a lurch, you and your friends are off for one more night on ~. town. S
epilogue.gigi: IE“ Gigi Survived”: The envelope that arrives is thick and perfumed. You remember the last time you received a letter like this—and in spite of everything, you still open it. Inside, there’s a message written in looping, self-assured script. “Paris is divine, darling. Met someone, too. Charming, dangerous. Real big arms.” Tucked behind the letter is a photograph. Gigi stands in front of the Eiffel Tower, one hand on her hip, the other draped possessively over the arm of a broad-shouldered man with foxlike eyes. “Boston's mine now,” the letter continues. “Funny how these things shake out. Don’t be strangers—or else! XOXOX” You stare at the photo a moment longer than you should. The idea of Gigi at the head of the Boston Mob is... surprising, to say the least. Maybe a little worrying. But when it comes to your new ‘business colleague,’ you've learned to anticipate surprises.
epilogue.declan:
The street outside is draped in fog, silver mist curling under the streetlight. But there, just beyond the glass of your window, stands a figure you know too well. Declan O’Doyle is still wearing the suit he died in, and his face is still as mangled as the night you found his body at the Hotel Seasons. His head tilts, neck bending too far. He grins.

Then, he raises one hand and reaches out, dirt-caked fingers tapping against the windowpane. Tap-tap-tap.

You can hear him laughing. There, in the condensation in your window, he’s written two words: “Thanks, Kid”

By the time you blink, the fog has swallowed him whole.
epilogue.stolas:
Months later, just as you’ve begun to put this entire ordeal behind you, you hear the flutter of wings from your kitchen. Somehow, you already know what will be waiting for you inside—who will be waiting for you. Stolas perches on the counter, talons curling into the porcelain.

“Well,” he says. Somehow, you aren’t surprised at all to hear him speak. “Look at you! A survivor.” His head tilts, feathers rippling in a slow, thoughtful wave. “Gratitude where it’s due—you’ve done me a favor larger than you know. I never did like that horrible woman.” He pauses, eyes narrowing to slits. “But I suspect you’re still hungry for more.”

He leans forward, gaze locking with yours. “So tell me, love. Shall we discuss a new contract?”

The air smells faintly of burnt parchment.
